segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He got into a boat, crossed over, and came to his own town.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, some people were bringing him a paralyzed man lying on a bed. Seeing their faith, Jesus said to the paralyzed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take courage, child; your sins are forgiven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, some of the scribes said to themselves,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is blaspheming.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: then he said to the paralyzed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get up, pick up your bed, and go to your house.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he got up and went off to his house.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the crowds saw it, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As Jesus went on from there, he saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he got up and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as he was reclining at table in the house, look, many tax collectors and sinners came and reclined with Jesus and his disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when he heard it, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Go and learn what this means: ‘I want mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I did not come to call the righteous but sinners.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then John’s disciples came to him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch pulls away from the garment, and a worse tear results.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Nor do people put new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise the skins burst, the wine pours out, and the skins are ruined. Instead, they put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was saying these things to them, look, an official came and bowed down before him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My daughter has just died. But come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus got up and followed him, and so did his disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, a woman who had been suffering from bleeding for twelve years came up behind him and touched the tassel of his cloak,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for she was saying to herself,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If I only touch his cloak, I will be made well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus turned and saw her, and he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take courage, daughter; your faith has made you well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the woman was made well from that hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus came to the official’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd in an uproar,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go away, for the girl has not died but is sleeping.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they laughed at him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl got up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this report went out into that whole region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Have mercy on us, Son of David!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had gone into the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you believe that I am able to do this?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes, Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he touched their eyes and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let it be done for you according to your faith.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “See that no one knows about this.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they went out and spread the news about him throughout that whole region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were going out, look, people brought to him a mute man who was possessed by a demon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when the demon had been driven out, the mute man spoke. The crowds were amazed and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Pharisees said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is by the ruler of the demons that he drives out demons.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus went around all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he saw the crowds, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.”

notes.note: This is Capernaum, where Jesus had settled according to Matthew 4:13, not Nazareth where he grew up. Mark’s parallel account names the town.
The SBLGNT reads “knowing.” Many manuscripts, followed by some other critical editions, have a very similar-looking Greek word meaning “seeing.” The sense is little affected either way.

This was a station where tolls and customs duties on goods were collected. The collectors worked under contract for the ruling authorities and were widely despised as dishonest and as collaborators. That is why “tax collectors and sinners” are paired in the verses that follow.

notes.phrase: I want mercy and not sacrifice
notes.traditional: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice
notes.note: Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6. In its original setting the saying is generally understood as a statement of priority rather than a rejection of the sacrificial system: loyal kindness matters more to God than ritual. Matthew has Jesus quote the same line again at 12:7.

The Greek is literally “sons of the bridal chamber,” a Semitic idiom for those who belong to the wedding party. It may mean the guests in general or more narrowly the bridegroom’s attendants. Most modern translations render it “wedding guests.”

The Greek word covers anyone holding a position of authority, from a magistrate to a local community leader, whereas “ruler” now suggests a sovereign. Mark and Luke identify the man as Jairus, a leader of the synagogue. The same Greek word is used in verse 34, where “ruler” of the demons fits the sense.

The Greek verb names the act of prostrating oneself in reverence, and its meaning depends on who receives it. Here a petitioner falls before Jesus to beg for help, and the scene contains no confession of divine status, so the gesture is translated rather than “worshiped.” Most modern versions do likewise (“knelt before him”), though scholars differ on how much recognition of Jesus Matthew intends in such scenes.

The word can mean simply the edge of a garment. It is also the Septuagint’s term for the tassels that Jewish men wore on the corners of their cloaks in obedience to Numbers 15:38–39, and Matthew uses it in that sense at 23:5. Many scholars think the tassel is meant here, though “edge” remains possible.

The Greek verb is the ordinary word for rescuing someone from danger or illness, and it is the same verb translated “save” elsewhere in the New Testament. It occurs three times in verses 21–22. Physical healing is in view here, but the link Jesus makes with faith may have suggested the wider sense to Matthew’s readers as well.

The Greek verb is passive in form and can mean either “got up” or “was raised.” It is also the usual New Testament verb for raising the dead. It is used of the paralyzed man in verses 5–7 and is rendered “got up” throughout the chapter, but “was raised” is equally possible here.

notes.phrase: It is by the ruler of the demons that he drives out demons
notes.note: This verse is missing from a few witnesses, including Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts, and some scholars suspect it was brought in from the similar charge at 12:24. The great majority of manuscripts include it, and the SBLGNT prints it without brackets.

The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, and was also used of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has become a religious term and a book title, which hides that everyday sense. Many modern translations already alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

candidates.reason: This narrative attention-marker is extremely frequent, and translators vary between “behold,” “look,” “just then,” “suddenly” and silent omission, so a single policy is needed.
In healing stories the verb is rendered “heal,” “make well” or “save” by different translators, and the link to “your faith has saved you” elsewhere is lost unless one policy is set.
The verb serves both for ordinary rising and for raising the dead, and its passive forms (“got up” or “was raised”) need a consistent policy, especially in healing and resurrection scenes.
Lexicographers argue that “toll collector” is more accurate than “tax collector,” and the older “publican” is obsolete; the term recurs across the Synoptic Gospels and should be uniform.
This word recurs across the Synoptics and is rendered variously as “had compassion,” “felt pity” or “was deeply moved,” so readers would lose the repeated motif if the English varies.

warnings: Verse 3: βλασφημέω is not rendered with a register form (slander; blaspheme; insult / hurl insults at / hurl insults) and has no register-exception note.
